title: Terminally Online
blurb: Five words that only mean what they mean because of the internet.

words.definition: Influence, especially the borrowed kind.
words.note: Originally a heavy blow — a clout round the ear. It meant force long before it meant followers, which is either a downgrade or exactly the same thing.

words.definition: Spreading fast and without permission.
words.note: We borrowed the word from epidemiology and kept the metaphor intact: something small, self-replicating, and not obviously good for you.

words.definition: Someone provoking a reaction for sport.
words.note: Not the bridge-dwelling monster. It comes from trolling, the fishing technique — dragging bait slowly behind a boat to see what bites.

words.definition: Admirably indifferent to what anyone thinks.
words.note: Coined by rapper Lil B, who took it back from an insult and made it a compliment. One of the few slang terms with a documented author.

words.definition: More replies than likes. A public verdict.
words.note: A cold mathematical term repurposed as one of the internet's cruellest judgements. Nobody announces their own ratio.

title: Red Flags
blurb: Things your friends noticed before you did.

words.definition: Poisonous, now mostly about people.
words.note: From the Greek toxikon, the poison Greek archers smeared on arrows. The word has always been about something aimed at you.

words.definition: To vanish rather than have the conversation.
words.note: The verb only dates to the 2010s, but it is a very old idea with a new name: the person is still there, just no longer visible to you.

words.definition: Small-minded, and enjoying it.
words.note: From the French petit, small. It meant literally minor before it meant deliberately so — the modern sense is almost a boast.

words.definition: Bitter about losing and showing it.
words.note: Likely from sailors, whose language and temperament were both described as salty long before anyone was salty in a group chat.

words.definition: Not quite honest, and not quite deniable.
words.note: Shade as an insult comes from Black and Latino ballroom culture, where throwing shade was an art form: the insult you could not quite prove.

title: Big Feelings
blurb: Precise names for things you have felt but not labelled.

words.definition: Warm, laughing happiness.
words.note: Shares a root with merry. It is specifically the sociable kind of joy — you can be happy alone, but mirth wants company.

words.definition: Fear of something not here yet.
words.note: The useful distinction: fear points at something present, dread points at the future. Dread is the more exhausting of the two.

words.definition: A small doubt that arrives uninvited.
words.note: Originally meant a sudden wave of sickness or faintness. The modern sense kept the physical suddenness and moved it into the conscience.

words.definition: Burning enthusiasm, usually for a person.
words.note: From the Latin ardere, to burn — the same root as arson. English kept the heat and dropped the damage.

words.definition: Dread with no particular object.
words.note: Taken whole from German, via Freud and Kierkegaard. English had no word for anxiety-about-nothing-specific, which is a strange gap for English to have had.

title: Money Moves
blurb: Five ways value changes hands, not all of them legal.

words.definition: A long con dressed as a business.
words.note: American carnival slang from around 1900. It implies patience — a grift is worked, not pulled.

words.definition: To accumulate well past the point of use.
words.note: Not the same as a horde, which is a crowd. One is treasure, the other is people, and they are unrelated words that sound identical.

words.definition: Anything you own that counts for something.
words.note: From the Anglo-French aver assetz, to have enough. The singular asset was reverse-engineered from assets, which came first.

words.definition: Payment for a decision.
words.note: Originally a piece of bread given to a beggar. It drifted from charity to theft to corruption in about three hundred years.

words.definition: A tenth, given whether you want to or not.
words.note: Literally the old English word for tenth. The number is baked into the word, which is why a nine percent tithe is a contradiction.

title: Doomscroll
blurb: It is 1am and you are still going.

words.definition: Consuming far more than intended, in one sitting.
words.note: A Lincolnshire dialect word meaning to soak a wooden vessel until it stopped leaking. The drinking sense came first; the television sense is very recent.

words.definition: Reads everything, posts nothing.
words.note: Lurker is one of the oldest pieces of internet slang, in use on Usenet by the early 1980s and essentially unchanged since.

words.definition: Short videos; also what your head does after.
words.note: A genuine double meaning: reel is film wound on a spool, and to reel is to stagger. Both apply.

words.definition: To flick aside. To steal.
words.note: The theft sense is nineteenth-century slang. That we now use the same gesture-word to dismiss people is a coincidence worth sitting with.

words.definition: A short puff of praise on a cover.
words.note: Invented in 1907 by humorist Gelett Burgess, who put a fictional Miss Belinda Blurb on a book jacket as a joke. The joke became the industry standard.

title: Worth Knowing
blurb: The quiet ones. You will use at least two of these.

words.definition: Something that soothes a wound.
words.note: Also a verb for easing a conscience — you salve your guilt. The physical and moral senses have run in parallel for a thousand years.

words.definition: The lowest possible point.
words.note: From the Arabic nazir, opposite — it is the astronomical point directly beneath you, exactly opposite the zenith. Arabic gave English most of its star vocabulary.

words.definition: The character of a group, as lived rather than stated.
words.note: One of Aristotle's three means of persuasion, alongside pathos and logos. Ethos is the argument that you are worth listening to.

words.definition: A small trained core inside a larger body.
words.note: From the French for frame — the cadre is the frame a larger organisation is built onto. Same root as cadre in painting: the thing around the picture.

words.definition: Understood without being said.
words.note: From the Latin tacere, to be silent — the same root as taciturn. A tacit agreement is binding precisely because nobody wrote it down.

title: Heartbreak
blurb: Five words for one bad week.

words.definition: To reject with contempt.
words.note: Originally meant to kick. The physical sense survives in the word's tone — to be spurned is worse than to be refused.

words.definition: A meeting arranged in secret.
words.note: Originally a hunting term: the appointed place where you waited for the game to be driven towards you. Make of that what you will.

words.definition: What is still warm after the fire.
words.note: An unusually old word, barely changed from Old English aemerge. It has always meant the part that outlasts the thing itself.

words.definition: To feel a loss openly.
words.note: Related to memory through an old root meaning to be anxious or remember. Mourning is etymologically an act of remembering, not of sadness.

words.definition: To want something distant, continuously.
words.note: Shares a root with the German gern, gladly. The ache and the gladness are the same word underneath, which feels about right.

title: Gym Rat
blurb: Posted at 5:40am so you would know.

words.definition: Visibly, deliberately muscular.
words.note: A deliberate misspelling of swollen, which is what it actually describes. Gym slang is unusually honest about mechanisms.

words.definition: Muscle, spoken of as property.
words.note: The countable plural is the giveaway — gains are treated as a possession you can lose, hence the fear of losing them.

words.definition: A cleanse with no medical meaning.
words.note: A real clinical term borrowed by the wellness industry. Your liver was already doing this, for free, the entire time.

words.definition: Physical force and liveliness.
words.note: From the Latin vigere, to be lively — the same root as vigil and vigilant. Staying awake and being strong were once the same idea.

words.definition: The point of the exercise.
words.note: One of the oldest words in English, cognate with the Sanskrit svedas. Humans have needed this word for as long as there have been words.

title: Old Words, New Energy
blurb: Medieval insults that deserve a comeback.

words.definition: To strike down, usually from above.
words.note: Also, bafflingly, to be smitten — struck by love. English decided being hit hard and falling in love warranted the same verb.

words.definition: A dishonest man of low standing.
words.note: Originally just meant boy, with no insult intended. It spent five hundred years sliding downhill, which is the usual fate of words for young men.

words.definition: Someone rude by disposition.
words.note: Meant a free peasant — a social rank, not a judgement. Churlish is what the upper classes decided that rank implied.

words.definition: A female fox. A woman with a temper.
words.note: One of the few English words preserving an old southern dialect habit of voicing an initial f into a v. Fixen became vixen and stuck.

words.definition: A likeable scoundrel; or something gone off-script.
words.note: Appeared suddenly in the 1560s with no clear ancestor. A word for people who go off on their own that itself came from nowhere.

title: Running on Empty
blurb: You are fine. You are definitely fine.

words.definition: Used up, with nothing held back.
words.note: The same word for money and for energy, which is not a metaphor English chose so much as one it never questioned.

words.definition: Damaged by too much heat, for too long.
words.note: Burnt and burned are both correct; British English tends to burnt for the adjective. Burnout borrowed the image wholesale in the 1970s.

words.definition: Unsteady and slightly unreal.
words.note: Origin genuinely unknown — it simply appears in American English in the 1890s. Possibly a blend of woozle and boozy, possibly nothing.

words.definition: To sleep suddenly and without ceremony.
words.note: The sleep sense comes from 1960s counterculture — crash pad predates crashing out. It has always implied you did not plan it.

words.definition: What is left at the bottom.
words.note: From Old Norse dregg. One of the many words Vikings left in English, alongside sky, knife, and — fittingly — ransack.
